# Chabbisodhana Sutta (MN 112 (PTS MN iii 29))

**ID:** MN 112 (PTS MN iii 29)
**Section:** Majjhimanikāya (mn)
**Collection:** Sutta
**Title (Pali):** Chabbisodhana Sutta
**Title (English, from literature):** The Sixfold Purification
**PTS:** MN iii 29
**tipitaka.org (CST):** https://tipitaka.org/romn/cscd/s0203m.mul1.xml

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Chabbisodhana Sutta* (MN 112; PTS MN iii 29) sets forth the procedure for interrogating and verifying a mendicant's claim to awakening (*arahantship*) [Anālayo, Scope of Free Inquiry; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka]. When a monk declares that he has attained arahantship, his claim is neither to be immediately accepted nor dismissed; instead, fellow practitioners should examine his realization with specific sets of detailed questions [Anālayo, Scope of Free Inquiry; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka]. Although the sutta's title announces an exposition of a "sixfold" purification, the extant Pali text details questions regarding only five topics: (1) four modes of communication or sense data (what is seen, heard, sensed, and cognized); (2) the five clinging aggregates; (3) the six internal and external elements (where the arahant neither identifies an element as self nor possesses a sense of self based on it); (4) the twelve sense bases; and (5) the body with consciousness together with all external signs [Anālayo 2014; Lin 2015; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka]. In outlining the path to destruction of the corruptions, the discourse depicts the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (*āsavakkhayañāṇa*) as being attained directly after the four *jhānas*, applying a fourfold analytical method to the *āsavas* (knowing them, their arising, their cessation, and the way leading to their cessation) [Anderson 1999; Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka].

**Sources**

- [Anālayo, Dawn of Abhidharma] Bhikkhu Anālayo, The Dawn of Abhidharma — Discusses textual loss in MN 112, the commentary's report of Indian monks' opinion, and comparison with MĀ 187.
- [Anālayo, Scope of Free Inquiry] Bhikkhu Anālayo, The Scope of Free Inquiry According to the Vīmaṃsaka-sutta — Notes the procedure adopted in MN 112 to verify the awakening claim of an arahant.
- [Lin 2015] Qian Lin, Mind in Dispute: The Section on Mind in Harivarman's Tattvasiddhi (2015) — Quotes the formula on diṭṭhe diṭṭhavāditā, sute sutavāditā, etc., from MN iii 29.
- [Anderson 1999] Carol S. Anderson, Pain and its Ending: The Four Noble Truths in the Theravada Buddhist Canon (1999) — Discusses the verbatim description of the destruction of the taints using the fourfold analysis of the āsavas.
- [Anālayo 2014] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Perspectives on Satipatthāna (2014) — Examines the arahant's lack of clinging and self-identification in regard to the elements in MN 112 compared to MĀ 187.
- [Wen, Study of Sukkhavipassaka] Tzungkuen Wen, A Study of Sukkhavipassaka in Pali Buddhism — Details the five questioning categories for verifying arahantship and the commentary's difficulty with the 'sixfold' title.
